newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget would reach surplus in 2002.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget would reach surplus in 2002.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday presented a $1.69 trillion budget that would cut $98.4 billion in taxes over five years, raise $76 billion in various taxes and fees, yet still reach balance by 2002.
The fiscal 1998 budget, which covers the year beginning on October 1, was formally released on Thursday after being widely leaked on Wednesday.
It forecast a 1998 deficit of $120.6 billion against 1997's $125.6 billion, gradually shrinking over the next three years and becoming a $17 billion surplus in 2002.
In putting forward the proposal, Clinton, a Democrat, was essentially presenting his opening offer in the annual budget negotiations between the president and the Republican-held Congress.
In doing so, he is returning to the primary battleground between the two parties since the Republicans won majority control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in 1994.

In a message accompanying the budget, Clinton noted that the budget deficit has been cut by more than 60 percent since he took office in 1993 and said he wanted to work with the Republicans to finish the job.

"Over the last four years, my administration and Congress have already done much of the hard work of reaching balance in 2002," Clinton said. "I want to work with Congress to achieve the final increment of deficit cutting and bring the budget into balance for the first time since 1969."
But initial reaction to the president's budget from Representative John Kasich, the influential Ohio Republican who chairs the House Budget Committee, was negative.

"The president of the United States, while declaring the era of big government at an end, every day comes up with another programme to actually expand government," Kasich told CNN in a televised interview.

The key differences between the two parties over the past two years have been over how much to cut taxes as well as how to reduce spending, particularly on popular "entitlements" like the Medicare health care programme for the elderly.

Clinton's budget proposed $98.4 billion in tax cuts over five years, chiefly to benefit families and promote education. It includes a $500 per child credit as well as a $1,500 tax credit or $10,000 tax deduction for college tuition.
It also would extend the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $500,000 per couple. At present, there is a $125,000 capital gains tax exclusion only for people over 55.

At the same time, the budget proposed raising $34.3 billion by closing corporate tax loopholes and extending expiring excise and other taxes worth $41.7 billion, leading to such tax revenue increases of $76 billion over five years.
To help cut the deficit, the government would also raise $36.1 billion from sales of broadcast spectrum licenses to private industry over the five years.
As previously reported, the budget would trim $100 billion over five years from projected spending on the popular, and politically sensitive, Medicare health care programme for the elderly.
Kasich specifically criticised the targeted nature of Clinton's tax cuts, and suggested the markets would not be impressed by the budget.

"If we're going to have tax relief for Americans why don't we let them decide what they want to spend that tax relief on and not make them have to do certain things that the government dictates," he said.
"Without solving many of the huge problems that are out there, the markets I don't believe are going to allow interest rates to come down," he added.
